title: Key technologies cheat sheet
scopeHtml:
Scope: what Redis, Kafka, Postgres, Cassandra, DynamoDB, Elasticsearch, S3, Nginx and ZooKeeper/etcd are for, their limits and sizing numbers.

Scope: what Redis, Kafka, Postgres, Cassandra, DynamoDB, Elasticsearch, S3, Nginx and ZooKeeper/etcd are for, their limits and sizing numbers.

notes.title: How to use this cheat sheet
notes.html:
For each technology know four things: what it is for, what it is bad at, its rough limits, and the back-of-envelope numbers. Numbers are order-of-magnitude on typical modern hardware; real values depend on hardware, version and workload. Always say "roughly" and offer to benchmark.

Handy constants: 1 day = 86,400 s (about 100k); 1M requests/day is about 12 requests/s; 1 KB x 1M rows = 1 GB; SSD random read about 100 us, HDD seek about 10 ms; 10 Gbps NIC is about 1.2 GB/s; peak is typically 2 to 3x average.

Tech Category Typical single-node ballpark
Redis In-memory KV/structures 100k ops/s, sub-ms
Kafka Distributed log 100s MB/s per broker
Postgres Relational OLTP 5k to 20k simple TPS
Cassandra Wide-column, AP 10k to 50k writes/s per node
DynamoDB Managed KV/doc Single-digit ms at any scale (partitioned)
Elasticsearch Search/analytics 1k to 10k queries/s per cluster tuned
S3 Object store Practically unlimited, 11 nines durability
Nginx Web server / proxy / LB 10k to 50k+ req/s per core class
ZooKeeper/etcd Coordination KV 1k to 10k writes/s, tiny data

Worked example. Interviewer says 50k reads/s. Redis cache hits can do it on one node; Postgres alone needs read replicas (50k / 10k = 5 replicas) or a cache with 90% hit rate (5k/s hits the DB).

Common interview traps.

  • Quoting numbers with no unit or context ("Redis is fast").
  • Picking a tech by hype instead of access pattern (read/write ratio, consistency need, data size).

notes.title: Redis
notes.html:
Redis is an in-memory data structure server: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps, HyperLogLog, geo, pub/sub. Single-threaded command execution (I/O threads since 6) gives atomic operations and about 100k ops/s per node, sub-millisecond latency.

Use for: cache, session store, rate limiter, leaderboards (sorted set), distributed lock (with caveats), queues (lists/streams), counters. Not for: primary storage of data you cannot lose, or datasets larger than RAM.

Limits and numbers:

  • Data must fit in RAM: 1M keys x 1 KB = about 1 GB (plus 50 to 100 B overhead per key). Practical node size 25 to 100 GB (fork for snapshots needs headroom).
  • Max value 512 MB (keep under 100 KB). Avoid KEYS *, big HGETALL, huge sets (blocks the single thread).
  • Persistence: RDB snapshots and AOF (appendfsync everysec loses up to ~1 s). Replication is async, so failover can lose recent writes.
  • Scaling: Redis Cluster splits keys into 16,384 hash slots over masters; multi-key ops only within a slot (hash tags {user42}). Sentinel for HA without sharding.
  • Eviction: maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru (cache) or noeviction.
SET session:abc '{"u":42}' EX 1800
ZADD leaderboard 1520 "alice"; ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES
SET lock:order:9 token NX PX 30000     # simple lock; use fencing tokens for correctness

Industry examples. Twitter timelines cached in Redis lists, Instagram media-id mappings, Snapchat and GitHub for queues and caches, Stack Overflow for caching.

Everyday analogy. A whiteboard in the office: instant to read and write, but if the power goes out you may lose the last scribbles, and it cannot hold the whole archive.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating Redis as durable (async replication, fsync policy).
  • Redlock as a safety guarantee for correctness (it is debated; use fencing or DB constraints).
  • Hot key melting one slot; fix with local cache or key splitting.

notes.title: Kafka
notes.html:
Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log: producers append, consumers read at their own offset, data is retained for days or forever. It decouples producers from consumers and gives replay.

Mechanism: a topic has N partitions; each is an ordered append-only log on a broker, replicated (replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all for no loss). Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition; the message key picks the partition. A consumer group gives each partition to one consumer, so parallelism is capped by partition count. Offsets are committed per group.

Numbers: one broker handles roughly 100 to 300 MB/s sequential writes (hundreds of thousands of msgs/s), end-to-end latency typically 5 to 50 ms, partitions per broker keep to low thousands, topic message size default 1 MB. Retention by time (retention.ms, for example 7 days) or size. Sizing: 50k msgs/s x 1 KB = 50 MB/s; x 3 replicas = 150 MB/s disk writes; 7 days = 30 TB raw before replication.

# producer for durability
acks: all
enable.idempotence: true
compression.type: lz4
linger.ms: 5
batch.size: 65536

Delivery semantics: at-least-once is default (commit after processing); exactly-once within Kafka via idempotent producer plus transactions; end-to-end needs idempotent consumers.

Industry examples. LinkedIn (origin, trillions msgs/day), Uber, Netflix (event pipelines), Slack, Swiggy/Zomato for order events. Pulsar and Kinesis are alternatives; RabbitMQ/SQS for classic task queues.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper archive: publishers keep adding issues; each reader keeps a bookmark and can reread old issues.

Common interview traps.

  • Expecting global ordering. Only per-partition, so choose the key (for example order_id).
  • More consumers than partitions (idle consumers).
  • Hot partition from a skewed key; too many partitions slowing recovery.
  • Using Kafka as a random-access database or per-message queue with priorities.

notes.title: PostgreSQL
notes.html:
Postgres is a mature relational database with ACID transactions, rich SQL, JSONB, extensions (PostGIS, pgvector) and strong consistency. Default choice for system-of-record data.

Mechanism: MVCC (readers do not block writers), WAL for durability and replication, B-tree indexes by default (also GIN, GiST, BRIN, hash), write-ahead streaming replication to read replicas (async by default, lag in ms to seconds), vacuum to reclaim dead rows. Process-per-connection model, so use PgBouncer (connection pooling) beyond a few hundred connections.

Numbers: a well-tuned node does about 5k to 20k simple TPS and 50k+ indexed point reads/s; single table comfortable to hundreds of millions of rows (1 TB+ DBs are common); max_connections 100 to 500 realistically (each about 10 MB); replication lag typically under 1 s. Row-sizes: 8 KB pages, TOAST for big values, keep rows under ~2 KB for density.

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_user_created ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC);
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

Scale path: indexes, then cache, then read replicas, then partitioning (declarative, by range or hash), then sharding (Citus, Vitess-like app sharding) as a one-way door.

Industry examples. Instagram scaled Postgres with sharding early on; Notion sharded Postgres by workspace id; Discord and Reddit run it; Stripe uses MongoDB and later sharded Postgres elsewhere (confirm details). Alternatives: MySQL (Vitess at YouTube/Slack), CockroachDB/Spanner for distributed SQL.

Everyday analogy. A well-run filing office with strict rules and a precise clerk: reliable and flexible, but one clerk's desk only gets so big.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting connection pooling (connection exhaustion is a classic outage).
  • Long transactions blocking vacuum (table bloat).
  • Reading from replicas right after writing (replication lag, read-your-writes bug).
  • Adding an index on a hot table without CONCURRENTLY.

notes.title: Cassandra
notes.html:
Cassandra is a masterless, wide-column store built for massive write throughput, linear horizontal scale and multi-datacenter availability. It trades flexible queries and strong consistency for those.

Mechanism: data is partitioned by partition key onto a consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes; each partition replicated RF=3. Writes go to commit log + memtable, flushed to immutable SSTables, merged by compaction (LSM tree), so writes are append-only and very fast. Tunable consistency: ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL; R + W > RF (for example QUORUM+QUORUM with RF=3) gives read-your-writes. You model tables per query (denormalise), no joins, limited secondary indexes.

Numbers: roughly 10k to 50k writes/s per node; nodes hold 1 to 2 TB comfortably (compaction limits density); keep partitions under ~100 MB / 100k rows; p99 reads in low ms. Tombstones (deletes) are a notorious problem: heavy deletes and TTL churn slow reads.

CREATE TABLE messages_by_chat (
  chat_id uuid, sent_at timeuuid, sender uuid, body text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id), sent_at)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (sent_at DESC);
-- Query: SELECT * FROM messages_by_chat WHERE chat_id=? LIMIT 50;

Industry examples. Netflix, Apple (hundreds of thousands of nodes), Discord (messages; later moved to ScyllaDB), Instagram (direct and feed), Uber. ScyllaDB is a C++ compatible rewrite.

Everyday analogy. A team of equal librarians, each owning shelves; anyone can take your delivery, they tell the others; no single boss to fail.

Common interview traps.

  • Using it for ad-hoc queries or heavy relational needs.
  • Unbounded partitions (a chat id that grows forever): add a time bucket to the partition key.
  • Counting on ALL for consistency and losing availability.

notes.title: DynamoDB
notes.html:
DynamoDB is AWS's fully managed key-value/document database with predictable single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale. You provision (or let on-demand scale) throughput; AWS handles partitioning, replication (3 AZs) and failover.

Mechanism: table has a partition key (hash) and optional sort key (range); items up to 400 KB. Data is split into partitions; each partition supports about 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU. RCU: one strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB per second (eventually consistent is half cost). WCU: one write up to 1 KB per second. GSI (global secondary index) lets other access patterns, eventually consistent, with their own throughput; LSI shares the partition key. Transactions (TransactWriteItems, up to 100 items), Streams (change capture), TTL, global tables (multi-region active-active, last-writer-wins), DAX (in-memory cache, microseconds).

Worked sizing: 10k writes/s of 2 KB items = 10k x 2 WCU = 20,000 WCU. 20k eventually consistent reads/s of 8 KB = 20k x (8/4) x 0.5 = 20,000 RCU. Hot partition: a single key above ~1,000 writes/s throttles, so spread keys (write sharding with a suffix key#0..9).

{ "TableName": "Orders",
  "KeySchema": [{"AttributeName":"pk","KeyType":"HASH"},{"AttributeName":"sk","KeyType":"RANGE"}],
  "BillingMode": "PAY_PER_REQUEST" }

Industry examples. Amazon.com cart and Prime Day (peaks above 100M requests/s), Lyft, Snapchat, Duolingo, Airbnb; Cassandra, MongoDB and Bigtable are similar families.

Everyday analogy. A giant locker room with instant key lookup; you may ask only "give me locker X" or "lockers X1 to X9", not "find lockers with red bags" unless you built an index in advance.

Common interview traps.

  • Designing as if it has joins or ad-hoc queries. You must know access patterns first.
  • Hot partition and uneven keys.
  • Forgetting costs (scans are expensive) and the 400 KB item limit.

notes.title: Elasticsearch
notes.html:
Elasticsearch is a distributed search and analytics engine built on Lucene: full-text search, relevance ranking, aggregations and log analytics. It is a secondary index, not your system of record.

Mechanism: an index is split into shards (primary + replicas); each shard is a Lucene index of immutable segments built around an inverted index (term to document list). Writes are near real time: a refresh (default 1 s) makes new docs searchable; merges compact segments. Queries fan out to all shards then merge (scatter-gather). Analyzers (tokenise, lowercase, stem) decide how text is matched. Also vector search (kNN) in recent versions.

Numbers: shard size target 10 to 50 GB; keep shard count per node low (a rule of thumb is under 20 shards per GB of heap); heap at most ~30 GB (compressed oops); cluster with 3 dedicated master nodes; ingest 5k to 50k docs/s per node depending on mapping; query latency 10 to 100 ms. Sizing: 100M docs x 1 KB = 100 GB x (1 + 1 replica) = 200 GB, roughly 4 to 10 shards.

PUT /products
{ "settings": {"number_of_shards": 5, "number_of_replicas": 1, "refresh_interval": "5s"},
  "mappings": {"properties": {"title": {"type": "text"}, "brand": {"type": "keyword"}, "price": {"type": "float"}}} }

Industry examples. Wikipedia and GitHub search, Uber and Netflix log/search platforms, the ELK/Elastic Stack for observability, Swiggy and Flipkart product search. Alternatives: OpenSearch (AWS fork), Solr, Typesense, Meilisearch, ClickHouse for analytics.

Everyday analogy. The index at the back of a book: instead of reading every page, look the word up and jump to the pages.

Common interview traps.

  • Using it as the primary database (no ACID, risk of data loss on bad mappings).
  • Deep pagination with from+size (use search_after).
  • Mapping explosion and too many small shards.
  • Forgetting indexing lag (not real-time-consistent with the DB).

notes.title: S3 and object storage
notes.html:
S3 stores immutable-ish blobs (objects) in buckets with massive durability and scalability; it is cheap, not low-latency. Use for images, video, backups, logs, data lakes, static websites.

Mechanism: flat namespace (key = path-like string); objects up to 5 TB, a single PUT up to 5 GB (use multipart upload above ~100 MB, parts 5 MB to 5 GB, up to 10,000 parts); 11 nines durability (99.999999999%) by multi-AZ replication; strong read-after-write consistency since Dec 2020; request rates roughly 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads/s per prefix (scale with prefixes); first-byte latency tens of ms. Storage classes: Standard, Infrequent Access, Glacier tiers (cheaper, retrieval delay), Intelligent-Tiering. Features: versioning, lifecycle rules, pre-signed URLs, event notifications, server-side encryption, cross-region replication.

Cost sense: Standard about $0.023 per GB-month (confirm current pricing); 100 TB = about $2,300/month; egress is the sneaky cost (about $0.09/GB to the internet), so front with a CDN.

aws s3 cp big.mp4 s3://acme-media/videos/ --storage-class STANDARD_IA
aws s3 presign s3://acme-media/videos/big.mp4 --expires-in 600

Industry examples. Dropbox (moved off S3 to its own Magic Pocket), Netflix (masters and encodes), Instagram photos, every data lake (S3 + Parquet + Athena/Spark). Equivalents: GCS, Azure Blob, MinIO, Ceph.

Everyday analogy. A huge self-storage warehouse: nearly infinite and cheap, but you ask the clerk for a box by label; you do not edit pages inside a box in place.

Common interview traps.

  • Using it as a filesystem (no append, rename is copy+delete, listing is slow).
  • Storing blobs in the SQL database.
  • Public buckets by accident (the most common cloud data leak).
  • Millions of tiny objects (request costs and listing overhead): batch them.

notes.title: Nginx
notes.html:
Nginx is a high-performance event-driven web server, reverse proxy, load balancer, TLS terminator and cache. One worker process handles thousands of connections with non-blocking I/O (epoll).

Uses: serve static files, reverse proxy to app servers, L7 load balancing (round robin, least_conn, ip_hash), TLS termination, HTTP/2 and gzip/brotli, rate limiting (limit_req), caching (proxy_cache), WebSocket proxying. Also L4 via the stream module.

Numbers: one modern core handles about 10k to 30k simple proxied requests/s, and tens of thousands of static responses; 10k to 100k+ concurrent connections per node (tune worker_connections, file descriptor limits ulimit -n); memory per idle connection a few KB; adds under 1 ms latency.

worker_processes auto;
events { worker_connections 20000; }
http {
  upstream app { least_conn; server 10.0.0.11:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s; server 10.0.0.12:8080; keepalive 64; }
  proxy_cache_path /var/cache/nginx keys_zone=c:100m max_size=10g inactive=10m;
  server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    location /static/ { root /var/www; expires 7d; }
    location /api/ { proxy_pass http://app; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Connection ""; proxy_read_timeout 30s; }
  }
}

Industry examples. Serves a large share of the web (Netflix Open Connect uses it on CDN boxes, Cloudflare built on it historically); alternatives HAProxy, Envoy (service mesh), Traefik, Caddy, cloud ALBs.

Everyday analogy. A very efficient receptionist who greets thousands of visitors at once and forwards each to the right department without waiting on any single one.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting keepalive to upstreams (a new TCP connection per request).
  • Open source Nginx has only passive health checks.
  • The proxy becomes a single point of failure (run pairs with keepalived/VIP or DNS).

notes.title: ZooKeeper and etcd
notes.html:
ZooKeeper and etcd are small, strongly consistent key-value stores for coordination: leader election, configuration, service discovery, distributed locks and membership. They are not general databases.

Mechanism: a cluster of 3 or 5 nodes runs a consensus protocol (ZooKeeper uses ZAB, etcd uses Raft). One leader orders all writes; a write commits once a majority (quorum) acknowledges, so 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure and 5 tolerate 2. Reads can be served by followers (possibly stale) or linearizable via the leader. Features: ZooKeeper has znodes, ephemeral nodes (vanish when the session dies, giving liveness) and watches; etcd has revisions, leases with TTL and watch streams (Kubernetes uses etcd as its brain).

Numbers: roughly 1k to 10k writes/s, data limit small (etcd default 2 GB, recommended up to 8 GB; ZooKeeper znode default max 1 MB, keep values tiny), needs low latency disks (fsync on every write: use SSD) and low-latency network; use odd node counts, 5 across 3 AZs is typical; do not span far regions because every write needs a quorum round trip.

etcdctl put /services/orders/10.0.0.4 up --lease=$(etcdctl lease grant 10 | awk '{print $2}')
etcdctl watch /services/orders --prefix

Industry examples. Kafka (ZooKeeper historically; KRaft replaces it in newer versions), HBase, Hadoop, Kubernetes (etcd), Consul (Raft), Google Chubby (the original), Patroni for Postgres failover.

Everyday analogy. A small committee that must agree before anything is written in the official minutes; slow for bulk data but never contradictory.

Common interview traps.

  • Using it as a data store or queue (small data, write-limited).
  • Even-sized clusters (4 tolerates only 1 failure, same as 3).
  • Split-brain misunderstandings: the minority side must stop serving writes.
  • Distributed locks without lease/fencing: a paused client can wake up still thinking it holds the lock.

notes.title: Choosing between them
notes.html:
Start from the access pattern and consistency need, then pick the simplest tool.

Need Pick Why
Source of truth, relations, transactions Postgres ACID, SQL
Sub-ms cache, counters, rate limits, leaderboards Redis In-memory structures
Event streaming, replay, decoupling Kafka Durable ordered log
Massive writes, always-on, geo-distributed Cassandra / DynamoDB Leaderless partitioned
Full-text, relevance, log search Elasticsearch Inverted index
Photos, video, backups, lake S3 Cheap, durable
Edge proxy, TLS, static, LB Nginx Event-driven
Leader election, config, locks etcd / ZooKeeper Consensus

A typical e-commerce stack: Postgres (orders), Redis (cart, cache), Kafka (events), Elasticsearch (product search), S3 + CDN (images), Nginx/ALB (edge), etcd (cluster state, via Kubernetes).

Worked example. Chat app, 50M DAU, 40 messages/day each: 2B messages/day, about 23k writes/s average, 70k peak. Messages: Cassandra/DynamoDB (partition by chat, sort by time). Presence: Redis. Fan-out and notifications: Kafka. Search: Elasticsearch. Media: S3. Metadata and billing: Postgres.

Decision gravity. Choosing the primary datastore is a near one-way door; caches, search indexes and queues are derived and easy to rebuild or swap. Prefer boring tech you can operate.

Common interview traps.

  • "Polyglot everywhere" with no operational story: each new datastore costs on-call load.
  • Dual writes to DB and search/cache with no reconciliation; use CDC or outbox.
  • Choosing NoSQL "for scale" when one Postgres would serve 10x the traffic.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Know the latency ladder and constants (86,400 s/day, 1M/day is about 12 per second, peak 2 to 3x).
  • Redis: in-memory, about 100k ops/s, atomic structures, not durable by default; Cluster has 16,384 slots.
  • Kafka: partitioned replicated log, ordering per partition, consumers capped by partitions, acks=all + idempotence for safety.
  • Postgres: default system of record, 5k to 20k TPS per node, use PgBouncer and replicas, sharding is a one-way door.
  • Cassandra: leaderless LSM, per-query tables, tunable consistency, watch partition size and tombstones.
  • DynamoDB: managed KV, 400 KB items, RCU/WCU math, avoid hot keys, design by access pattern.
  • Elasticsearch: inverted-index search, 10 to 50 GB shards, secondary index only, near-real-time.
  • S3: 11 nines, 5 TB objects, multipart, pre-signed URLs, egress costs, CDN in front.
  • Nginx: event-driven proxy, TLS, LB, cache; keepalive upstream; avoid being a single point of failure.
  • ZooKeeper/etcd: Raft/ZAB quorum for locks, leader election, config; small data, odd cluster size, fencing tokens.

questions.promptHtml: Why is Redis fast, what is it good and bad at, and how durable is it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Redis appears in most designs; seniors know its limits (RAM, single thread, durability).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Redis keeps data in memory and runs commands on a single thread (atomic, no locks), giving about 100k ops/s per node at sub-millisecond latency. Great for caches, sessions, counters, rate limits, leaderboards. Bad as the only copy of data you cannot lose or for datasets bigger than RAM. Durability is optional via RDB snapshots and AOF, and replication is asynchronous.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Data structures: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps, HyperLogLog, geo.
  • Single-threaded command execution means one slow command (KEYS *, huge HGETALL, big SMEMBERS) blocks everyone.
  • Capacity: 1M keys x 1 KB is about 1 GB plus 50 to 100 B overhead per key; practical node 25 to 100 GB (fork for snapshots needs headroom).
  • Scaling: Redis Cluster shards into 16,384 hash slots; replicas for read scaling and failover (Sentinel or cluster).
  • Persistence: RDB (periodic snapshot, can lose minutes), AOF with everysec (lose about 1 s), async replication can lose acknowledged writes on failover.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
redis-cli SET session:42 "{...}" EX 3600
redis-cli ZADD leaderboard 1500 alice
redis-cli ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 9 WITHSCORES

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Redis as the system of record.
  • KEYS * in production (use SCAN).
  • Distributed locks with a single node and no fencing token, assuming they are safe.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Max value size? -> 512 MB, keep under about 100 KB.
  2. What happens on memory full? -> Depends on maxmemory-policy: evict (LRU/LFU) or reject writes (noeviction).
  3. Cluster multi-key operations? -> Only within one hash slot (use hash tags).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "it's an in-memory cache". Senior: single-thread implications, memory sizing, persistence and failover loss windows, cluster constraints.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams lose sessions or counters because eviction policy or failover assumptions were never examined.

questions.promptHtml: How do you use rough throughput numbers (for Redis, Kafka, Postgres and so on) in a design discussion without sounding like you are guessing?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Interviewers want order-of-magnitude reasoning with stated assumptions, not memorised exact figures.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I convert the requirement to per-second numbers (1M requests/day is about 12 rps, peak 2 to 3x), compare to per-node ballpark capacity, state the assumption, and add headroom. I say "roughly" and name what I would benchmark. Then I pick the technology whose limit I am safely below.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Handy constants: 1 day is about 86,400 s (about 100k); 1 KB x 1M rows = 1 GB; SSD random read about 100 us; HDD seek about 10 ms; 10 Gbps is about 1.2 GB/s.

Worked example: 50k reads/s requested.

Postgres node: ~10k simple reads/s  -> 5 replicas for 50k
Redis cache at 90% hit: 5k/s reach DB -> one Postgres node, 45k/s served by Redis (1 node ~100k ops/s)

Then state the knock-on effects: cache invalidation complexity, stampede protection.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting a number without unit or context ("Redis is fast").
  • Treating average as peak.
  • Forgetting replication, headroom (run at 50 to 70% of capacity) and failure of one node.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. 100M DAU, 10 requests each, peak? -> 1B/day is about 12k rps average, peak about 30k to 40k.
  2. Storage for 1B rows of 500 B? -> 500 GB before indexes and replication.
  3. Which number would you verify first? -> The one that decides the architecture, such as write rate per node.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: recites numbers. Senior: derives load, checks the design against node limits with headroom, and says what to load test.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Capacity plans without a peak factor lead to outages on the first marketing push.

questions.contextHtml:
Product catalog service uses one Redis node (24 GB used, 80k ops/s). Every few minutes API p99 jumps from 5 ms to 1.5 s for about 3 seconds. Evidence:

redis-cli --latency-history  -> spikes to 1,400 ms
SLOWLOG GET: HGETALL catalog:category:all   duration 1,380,000 us   (hash with 1.8M fields)
INFO: latest_fork_usec 900000 (during BGSAVE every 5 min)
used_memory 24 GB, host RAM 32 GB, transparent_hugepage enabled

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Redis is slow, add a node." Misses the big key and the fork latency.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who runs HGETALL and how often? Is persistence needed? Is THP on?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the caller doing HGETALL on that key (feature flag); move snapshots to a replica.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) a 1.8M-field hash read in one command blocks the single thread for 1.4 s; (2) BGSAVE fork of 24 GB takes 0.9 s with THP copy-on-write overhead; (3) network (no, SLOWLOG shows server time).
  4. How I'd verify: SLOWLOG, --bigkeys or MEMORY USAGE, INFO persistence, correlate spike times with save and the cron job.
  5. Root cause: A single-threaded server cannot absorb long commands or long forks.
  6. Fix: Break the big hash into buckets (catalog:category:{n}) or use HSCAN, move the full-list read to an application cache or a precomputed blob, disable THP, snapshot on a replica, keep memory below about 60% of the host for fork headroom, use UNLINK instead of DEL for large keys.
  7. Prevention: Alert on SLOWLOG entries over 10 ms and on key size, code review rule against unbounded collection reads, latency monitor.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sharding the hash adds client logic. I would not just scale vertically; the big key will still block.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is AOF better? -> Different cost (fsync, rewrite); still forks for rewrite.
  • Cluster help? -> Only if the keys are spread; one key lives on one shard.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "get all" admin export ran on the primary and froze checkout for two seconds each time.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Add nodes.
  • Hire: Finds big key and fork.
  • Strong hire: Fixes both, THP, replica snapshots, alerts and code rule.

questions.contextHtml:
An order-events topic has 12 partitions. Producers write 25k msgs/s (1 KB each, 25 MB/s). A consumer group of 20 pods processes each message in about 8 ms (calls a payment API). Lag grows 40k per minute and notifications arrive 25 minutes late.

kafka-consumer-groups --describe:
partition 0-11 LAG  ~(rising)   CONSUMER-ID: assigned to 12 pods; 8 pods have no partitions
max.poll.interval.ms=300000, session timeouts: rebalances every few minutes
questions.promptHtml: Why is lag growing and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more consumer pods." Pods beyond the partition count sit idle.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is ordering needed per key? Can processing be parallelised in a pod? Why do rebalances occur?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise per-pod concurrency (thread pool) if ordering per key is kept; scale the downstream API; pause non-critical consumers; increase partitions if keys allow.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) capacity: 12 partitions x (1000/8 = 125 msgs/s per consumer thread) = 1,500 msgs/s versus 25,000 in; (2) rebalances stalling consumption; (3) a slow downstream (the 8 ms may include retries).
  4. How I'd verify: Consumer lag per partition, processing time histogram, rebalance logs, API latency.
  5. Root cause: Parallelism is capped by partitions (max consumers in a group = partitions) and each consumer is serial with 8 ms of I/O per message. Needed throughput 25k/s requires about 200 concurrent in-flight (25,000 x 0.008).
  6. Fix: In each consumer, process with an async/concurrent pool (about 20 concurrent per pod x 12 pods = 240) preserving per-key ordering by key-hashing to worker queues; batch API calls if supported; increase partitions to 48 (plan: changing partition count remaps keys); tune max.poll.records and poll interval to stop rebalances; commit offsets after processing.
  7. Prevention: Alert on lag growth rate and time-lag, capacity formula in the runbook (throughput x latency = concurrency), load test.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: More partitions mean more overhead and break key-to-partition order across the change. I would not auto-commit before processing (data loss).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Poison message? -> Retry topic and dead-letter queue.
  • Exactly-once? -> Idempotent consumers plus transactional offsets; end-to-end needs idempotent side effects.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team scaled consumers from 12 to 60 pods to fix lag and only increased the bill.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: More pods.
  • Hire: Partition cap and concurrency math.
  • Strong hire: Little's law, ordering-preserving concurrency, rebalance tuning and DLQ.

questions.contextHtml:
A Postgres primary (16 vCPU, 64 GB, max_connections=500) serves 60 app pods, each with a pool of 20 connections. During a sale, errors begin:

FATAL: sorry, too many clients already
pg_stat_activity: 497 connections, 410 state='idle in transaction'? no: 410 'idle', 70 'active', 17 'idle in transaction'
load average 38, cpu 100%, TPS 9k, p99 query 900 ms

The team's reaction: raise max_connections to 2000.
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate that and propose the right fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Agrees to raise max_connections, which increases memory (about 10 MB per connection) and context switching.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are pools sized per pod? Any long transactions? Is PgBouncer available? Read/write split?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Reduce pool size per pod (20 to 5), kill idle in transaction sessions, throttle non-essential jobs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) 60 x 20 = 1,200 potential connections versus 500 allowed; (2) with 16 cores, only about 30 to 50 active queries are useful, the rest just wait; (3) idle-in-transaction sessions hold locks and snapshots, delaying vacuum.
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_activity, pg_locks, pg_stat_statements for top queries, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
  5. Root cause: Connection count is not the same as throughput. Each backend is a process (about 10 MB); beyond a few times the core count they add contention, not work.
  6. Fix: PgBouncer in transaction pooling (many client connections to about 50 server connections), pool per pod of 5, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement timeouts, optimise the top queries, add read replicas for reads. Raising to 2000 would use about 20 GB RAM just for backends and likely slow things.
  7. Prevention: Connection budget formula (pods x pool <= pooler limit), alert at 70% of connections, load test at peak pod count.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Transaction pooling breaks session features (prepared statements across transactions, advisory locks, SET), so check ORM usage. I would not raise max_connections first.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Autoscaling pods multiplies connections? -> Pooler decouples them.
  • Why is CPU 100% with mostly idle sessions? -> The 70 active queries (and bad plans) saturate 16 cores.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Autoscaling doubled pods during an incident and doubled the connection storm too.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Raise max_connections.
  • Hire: PgBouncer and pool sizing.
  • Strong hire: Connection budget math, idle-in-transaction timeouts, transaction pooling caveats.

questions.contextHtml:
A DynamoDB table events (partition key tenant_id, sort key ts) has 20,000 WCU provisioned. Writes of 2 KB items average 9,000/s but throttle at peak:

WriteThrottleEvents rising; ConsumedWriteCapacity 14,000 of 20,000 WCU
Contributor Insights: tenant_id=acme = 78% of writes (about 7,000 writes/s = 14,000 WCU)
per partition limit: about 1,000 WCU
questions.promptHtml: Why throttling at 70% utilisation and how to fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Raises provisioned capacity; the hot partition still caps at about 1,000 WCU.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do queries always scope by tenant? Is on-demand mode acceptable? Is ordering by ts per tenant required?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Short-term: batch or buffer writes through SQS/Kafka to smooth bursts; contact AWS support only after redesign since adaptive capacity helps but has limits.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) hot partition: one tenant writes 7,000 items/s x 2 WCU = 14,000 WCU against about 1,000 per partition; (2) table-level capacity is fine; (3) item size above 1 KB doubles WCU (2 KB = 2 WCU).
  4. How I'd verify: CloudWatch per-key metrics, Contributor Insights, throttled key list.
  5. Root cause: Partition key with low cardinality or skew for one tenant; capacity is per partition, not just per table.
  6. Fix: Write sharding: pk = tenant_id#(hash(ts) mod N) with N = 16 or more so 14,000 WCU spreads to under 1,000 per shard; reads then query N shards in parallel and merge (scatter-gather); or use a better key like tenant_id#date#shard. Reduce item size (compress, store payload in S3) to cut WCU. Consider on-demand mode for unpredictable load, at a higher unit cost (verify).
  7. Prevention: Key design review by access pattern, load test with skewed tenants, alarms on single-key share.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Sharding complicates reads and ordering. I would not rely on adaptive capacity as a design.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Strongly consistent read cost? -> 1 RCU per 4 KB; eventual is half.
  • Need per-tenant ordering? -> Sort within shards and merge by timestamp.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One enterprise customer's nightly import throttled every tenant sharing the table.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: More WCU.
  • Hire: Hot partition identification and key sharding.
  • Strong hire: WCU math, read fan-in cost, on-demand trade-off and payload reduction.

questions.promptHtml: How does Cassandra store and distribute data, and how do you model tables for it? What are tombstones and why are they a problem?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cassandra rewards query-first modelling and punishes relational habits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cassandra is a leaderless, AP wide-column store. Data is partitioned by the partition key on a consistent-hash ring with replication factor 3, writes go to a commit log and memtable then flush to immutable SSTables merged by compaction. You design one table per query, keep partitions bounded, and avoid heavy deletes because deletes write tombstones that slow reads until compaction purges them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
CREATE TABLE messages_by_chat (
  chat_id uuid, ts timeuuid, sender uuid, body text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id), ts)) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC);
-- SELECT * FROM messages_by_chat WHERE chat_id=? LIMIT 50;
  • Numbers: roughly 10k to 50k writes/s per node; 1 to 2 TB per node; keep partitions under about 100 MB or 100k rows.
  • Tunable consistency: QUORUM reads + writes with RF=3 gives overlap (R + W > RF).
  • Tombstones: a delete or TTL expiry is a marker kept for gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days) so replicas converge; reads scan them and can hit warnings or timeouts if thousands accumulate in one partition.
  • Unbounded partitions (one chat forever) get huge; bucket by time: (chat_id, month).
  • No joins, limited secondary indexes; denormalise.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Queue-like patterns (insert then delete) generating tombstones.
  • Modelling like SQL and using ALLOW FILTERING.
  • Low-cardinality partition keys causing hot nodes.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. QUORUM math? -> RF=3: quorum 2; read 2 + write 2 overlaps.
  2. Why writes are fast? -> Append-only commit log and memtable, no read-before-write.
  3. Lightweight transactions? -> Paxos-based, much slower; use sparingly.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "NoSQL for scale". Senior: query-driven tables, partition bounding, tombstones, consistency math and operational limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A job queue on Cassandra slowed to a crawl once tombstones piled up in hot partitions.

questions.contextHtml:
Product search cluster: 6 data nodes (64 GB RAM, 30 GB heap each). A daily index per tenant creates 14,000 indices, 5 primary shards each with 1 replica (140,000 shards); the data is only 900 GB total. Symptoms:

GET _cluster/health  -> status yellow, number_of_pending_tasks 4,800
master node: heap 92%, cluster state 380 MB, GC pauses 6 s
search p99 2.8 s; indexing rejected with es_rejected_execution_exception
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you restructure?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add nodes and heap." Treats a shard-count problem as a capacity problem.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Query patterns (tenant filter, time range)? Retention? Do tenants need isolation? Search freshness requirement?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop creating new tiny indices; close or delete old indices per retention; raise master heap carefully; add dedicated master nodes (3).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) oversharding: 140k shards for 900 GB is about 6 MB per shard against a rule of about 10 to 50 GB; (2) cluster state huge (mappings x indices) overloading master; (3) per-shard overhead (heap per shard) on data nodes.
  4. How I'd verify: _cat/shards, _cluster/stats, _cat/indices?s=store.size, heap per node.
  5. Root cause: Index-per-tenant-per-day with default 5 shards, treating an index like a table.
  6. Fix: Consolidate: shared indices with a tenant_id filter (or routing by tenant) and rollover by size (about 30 GB per shard) via ILM; 900 GB / 30 GB gives about 30 primary shards. Use _shrink/reindex for existing data, filtered aliases per tenant. 3 dedicated masters. Tune refresh_interval (5 s or 30 s during bulk) and bulk size.
  7. Prevention: Index templates with sane defaults, ILM policies, alerts on shard count per node and cluster state size.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Shared indices weaken tenant isolation and make large-tenant deletes harder; for a few huge tenants keep dedicated indices. I would not use dynamic mappings with user-defined fields (mapping explosion).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is Elasticsearch the source of truth? -> No; keep a primary DB and rebuild the index from it.
  • Near-real-time? -> Documents are searchable after a refresh (default 1 s).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A well-meaning index-per-customer design worked for 50 customers and died at 5,000.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Add nodes.
  • Hire: Spots oversharding, consolidates.
  • Strong hire: Shard sizing math, ILM, routing, cluster state and tenancy trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml: A video app stores 800 TB in S3 Standard and serves downloads directly from S3 to the internet. Monthly bill: storage about $18,000, egress about $140,000 (verify current prices; roughly $0.023 per GB-month storage and $0.09 per GB egress). Mobile uploads of 2 GB videos fail often over flaky networks and are retried from byte zero; support complains.
questions.promptHtml: How do you cut cost and fix uploads?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Moves to a cheaper storage class only; egress is the main cost.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Access pattern (how much is hot)? Geography of viewers? Is content cacheable? Compliance needs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Put a CDN in front immediately (with origin access control) so repeated downloads hit the edge.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) egress dominates: 140,000 / 0.09 is roughly 1.5 PB per month; (2) hot content is a small share and cacheable; (3) old videos in Standard are rarely read.
  4. How I'd verify: S3 server access logs or CloudFront reports by object, popularity curve, S3 Storage Lens.
  5. Root cause: Serving popular static objects straight from the origin and storing cold data in the hot tier.
  6. Fix: CDN with high cache hit ratio (if 85% hits, egress from S3 drops 85%; CDN egress is cheaper per GB, verify), lifecycle rules to Infrequent Access or Glacier tiers for old content (retrieval fees apply), intelligent tiering where access is unpredictable. Uploads: multipart upload with presigned URLs, 8 to 64 MB parts, parallel parts, retry only failed parts, abort incomplete multipart uploads with a lifecycle rule (they cost storage). Cross-region replication only where needed.
  7. Prevention: Cost dashboards by prefix, budget alerts, tagging, lifecycle in IaC.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Colder tiers have retrieval fees and latency; do not move hot content. Do not proxy uploads through your servers (bandwidth and CPU).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Large number of small objects? -> Request costs and per-request latency; batch or pack.
  • Consistency? -> S3 offers strong read-after-write consistency.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Unfinished multipart uploads accumulated 40 TB of invisible storage for months.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Storage class only.
  • Hire: CDN and lifecycle.
  • Strong hire: Cost math from the bill, multipart design, abort rules and tier trade-offs.

questions.contextHtml:
Nginx fronts 12 app pods; at 35k rps during a promotion users see intermittent 502/504:

error.log: 2026/11/13 12:04:11 [alert] 31#31: 1024 worker_connections are not enough
error.log: upstream prematurely closed connection while reading response header
error.log: connect() failed (99: Cannot assign requested address) while connecting to upstream
worker_processes 4; worker_connections 1024; no keepalive to upstream; ulimit -n 1024
ss -s: TIME-WAIT 61,000

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart Nginx and add pods."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is upstream keepalive enabled? How many concurrent clients? What are timeouts? Is Nginx CPU saturated?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise worker_connections and file descriptors, add Nginx instances behind the LB, reload (not restart).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) connection limit: each proxied request uses two connections (client and upstream); 4 x 1024 = 4,096 total, far below need; (2) no upstream keepalive: a new TCP connection per request exhausts ephemeral ports (the "cannot assign requested address", TIME-WAIT 61k); (3) upstream pods closing idle connections (premature close).
  4. How I'd verify: ss -s, netstat states, nginx -T, stub_status active connections, ulimit -n of the worker process.
  5. Root cause: Defaults sized for small traffic plus connection-per-request to upstream.
  6. Fix:
# nginx.conf (shown as key settings)
worker_processes: auto
worker_rlimit_nofile: 200000
events: { worker_connections: 50000 }
upstream app: { keepalive: 256 }          # with proxy_http_version 1.1 and proxy_set_header Connection ""

Also set upstream keepalive timeout lower than the app's idle timeout, tune net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, set sensible proxy_connect_timeout, proxy_read_timeout, and limit_req for abuse. 7. Prevention: Monitor active connections vs limit, load test with realistic concurrency, config in version control with sizing notes. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Huge timeouts hide slow upstreams and tie up connections. Do not enable tcp_tw_recycle-style hacks; use keepalive.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Capacity per node? -> Roughly 10k to 30k proxied requests/s per core class (verify by test).
  • WebSockets? -> Long-lived connections count against worker_connections.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single missing proxy_http_version 1.1 meant upstream keepalive was configured but silently unused.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Restart and add pods.
  • Hire: Raises limits, enables keepalive.
  • Strong hire: Explains two connections per request, ephemeral port exhaustion, timeouts alignment and capacity testing.

questions.contextHtml:
A team uses a 3-node etcd cluster for leader election and config, and has also begun storing per-user feature flags (6M keys, 4 GB) plus high-frequency heartbeats (8,000 writes/s). Symptoms:

etcdserver: request timed out; "apply request took too long" 1.2s
mvcc: database space exceeded  (quota 8 GB)
wal_fsync_duration p99 = 210 ms (disk shared with other workloads, HDD-backed volume)
leader changes: 14 in the last hour; services lose leadership and flap
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and what is the right architecture?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increases the quota and adds nodes. More members add write latency, not capacity.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What needs strong consistency? Which data is large or write-heavy? What disks back etcd?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Compact and defragment, disable alarm after freeing space; stop the heartbeat writer; move etcd to a dedicated SSD.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) misuse: etcd is a coordination store with small data and about 1k to 10k writes/s, not a feature-flag database; (2) slow disk fsync (210 ms) causes timeouts and leader elections; (3) revision history growth without compaction.
  4. How I'd verify: etcdctl endpoint status, metrics etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds, etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total, DB size vs keys.
  5. Root cause: Each write goes through Raft and fsync on a majority; the cluster is only as fast as its slowest quorum disk. Large keyspace plus heartbeat writes plus HDD pushed it past limits.
  6. Fix: Move feature flags to a proper store (Redis/DB with a cache pushed to services); use leases with TTLs and watch for election, not heartbeats via writes; dedicated fast SSD, 3 or 5 members (odd), regular compaction and defrag, keep data in the single-digit GB. Services cache config and keep working if etcd is briefly unavailable.
  7. Prevention: Alerts on fsync latency (target p99 under 10 ms), db size at 70% of quota, leader change rate; review rule: only small, rarely-changing coordination data.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A 5-node cluster tolerates 2 failures but writes get slower; don't add nodes for throughput. Do not place etcd on shared slow disks.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why odd numbers? -> Majority quorum; 4 nodes tolerate no more failures than 3.
  • ZooKeeper equivalent? -> Same principle: ephemeral znodes and watches; keep znodes tiny (default 1 MB cap).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Leader flapping caused a cascading failover storm in every service using etcd for locks.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: More nodes and quota.
  • Hire: Moves bulk data out, fixes disk.
  • Strong hire: Raft/fsync reasoning, election design with leases, compaction and fail-static clients.

questions.promptHtml: Given a chat app with 50M DAU sending 40 messages/day each, how do you pick the data stores and what do the numbers tell you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is the core HLD skill: derive load, map each need to the right tool, justify with limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: 50M x 40 = 2B messages/day, about 23k writes/s average and about 70k at peak. That is beyond one Postgres node, so messages go in a partitioned store (Cassandra or DynamoDB) keyed by chat and time. Presence and counters in Redis, fan-out and async work on Kafka, search in Elasticsearch fed from Kafka, attachments in S3 behind a CDN, coordination (leader election) in etcd or ZooKeeper, and Postgres for accounts and billing.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
2B msg/day / 86,400 = ~23k/s ; peak x3 = ~70k/s
storage: 2B x 1 KB = 2 TB/day => ~730 TB/year before replication (x3)
Messages  -> Cassandra/DynamoDB   (partition chat_id, sort by time; 70k writes/s = ~5-10 nodes at 10k/node, with RF=3 more)
Presence  -> Redis                (sub-ms, TTL keys)
Events    -> Kafka                (fan-out, notifications, indexing)
Search    -> Elasticsearch        (secondary index, rebuilt from the log)
Media     -> S3 + CDN
Accounts  -> Postgres             (strong consistency, relational)
  • Each choice follows a limit: Postgres 5k to 20k TPS per node, Redis RAM-bound, Cassandra tombstones/partition size, DynamoDB hot partitions and cost per WCU, Elasticsearch is not a source of truth.
  • Decision gravity: picking the message store is a one-way door (migration is expensive); search and cache are two-way.
  • Say what you would benchmark: write latency at peak, partition skew (very large group chats).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One database for everything.
  • Ignoring replication factor and peak in sizing.
  • Using Redis or Elasticsearch as the primary store.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not Postgres with sharding? -> Possible, but you operate the sharding yourself (one-way door); wide-column stores give it natively.
  2. Very large group chat (1M members)? -> Hot partition and fan-out problem; separate path and fan-out on read.
  3. How do you keep search consistent? -> Index from Kafka asynchronously; accept lag of seconds, rebuild from the source of truth.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: names a tool per box. Senior: derives the numbers, states per-node limits, notes failure modes and one-way doors, and what to verify.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that start with a single Postgres and defer the partitioning decision pay a painful migration at 10x growth.
